newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine March inflation up on wages, oil prices.
newsitem.headline: Philippine March inflation up on wages, oil prices.

text.p: The Philippines' year-on-year inflation rose to 4.8 percent in March from 4.4 percent in February because of the delayed impact of February's increase in wages and fuel prices, analysts said on Friday.

The March figure turned out be higher than the 4.6 percent rate expected by six securities firms and banks polled by Reuters. However, it was still below the 5.8 percent target of the Philippine Central Bank for March.
"This is the delayed impact from what happened in February," said Emma Pante, economist at Far East Bank.
"Price pressures are gradually being built up from wages and the oil price increases," said Lito Dalit, an economist of AsianBank Corp.

Analysts said these pressures were reflected in higher prices in the food, fuel, light and water components of the inflation index. Food makes up 53.5 percent of the index, while fuel, light and water together comprise 5.4 percent.
The National Statistics Office (NSO) reported that the price of rice, a major component of the food basket, increased by 1.6 percent in March compared with 0.3 percent in February.

The price gain in rice occurred despite sufficient stores of the staple. National Food Authority administrator Vic Racho told Reuters on Friday there were no problems in rice supply and distribution in March. He also said the country had 298,000 tonnes of rice, enough for 72 days.
Prices of fruits, vegetables, meat and fish also rose.
The country's oil refiners raised prices of certain petroleum products when the industry was freed from government control on February 8.
In addition, a government panel raised the 165-peso ($6.30) daily minimum wage in the capital region by 20 pesos, the first 15 pesos of which took effect in February.
Analysts said the impact of the increases had been slow because of the high level of competition in the Philippines' open economy.
Helen Alvarez, research director of All Asia Capital and Trust Corp, said inflation will edge up to 5.0 percent in the second quarter.
"We're still likely to feel the effect of the increase in basic utilities," she said, adding that prices of certain petroleum products could rise this month in line with regional prices.
Meanwhile, the March inflation rate will not have an impact on interest rates, analysts said.
Dalit of AsianBank said "interest rates should hold at current levels".
The Central Bank earlier on Friday said it remained confident its inflation target of six to seven percent this year would be easily reached. Inflation was 8.4 percent for all of 1996.
In March this year, the benchmark 91-day Treasury bill rate returned to single digits for the first time since September 1995 because of prevailing low inflation and ample liquidity in the system.
The 91-day T-bill rate fell to 9.498 percent on Monday from 9.724 percent the previous week. ($1 = 26.30 pesos)
